source.title: Stationary solutions of the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system: present status and open problems

accepted.question_text: Can analytic methods prove the existence of stationary axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov solutions that are far from spherical symmetry, meaning solutions whose spatial density and net angular momentum are not merely small perturbations of known spherical or low-angular-momentum solutions, including solutions that contain ergoregions?
accepted.context_brief: Analytic existence far from spherical symmetry

evidence.quote: These analytic results rely on a perturbation argument with the consequence that the constructed solutions can only be guaranteed to deviate slightly from spherically symmetric solutions and to have small total angular momentum.

Hence solutions which are far-from spherically-symmetric in the sense of spatial density and net angular momentum –in particular, solutions containing ergoregions– are not covered by these results. Accordingly, there is extensive room for analytic progress on the existence of stationary solutions.

accepted.question_text: For the numerical fixed-point construction of static or stationary Vlasov steady states, can one prove that the iteration map has a fixed point? In the simplified Vlasov-Poisson setting, the map takes an input spatial density ρ, computes its gravitational potential Uρ, substitutes Uρ into a prescribed particle ansatz Φ(E,L), renormalizes the resulting density to the prescribed total mass M by an amplitude K, and returns T(ρ)=K(ρ̃)ρ̃. The same fixed-point question should be settled for the spherically symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system and for the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system.

evidence.quote: We now define an amplitude K(˜ρ) = M (∫ ˜ρ(x) dx)−1 so that the new spatial density K(˜ρ) ˜ρ again has mass M. Let us consider the map T : D → D defined by T (ρ) = K(˜ρ)˜ρ.

It is an open problem to show that the map T has a fixed point. Similar fixed point problems, based on the same strategy, can be formulated for several related systems; e.g. the spherically symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system and the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system. It is an open problem in each case to show the existence of a fixed point.

accepted.question_text: Can the same fixed-point iteration method be used to construct new flat steady states of the Vlasov-Poisson system, especially steady states relevant as Newtonian disk-galaxy models, where existing results are limited?

evidence.quote: We have not only in mind the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system but also in the case of the Vlasov-Poisson system there is hope that this method can be used to construct new solutions, namely flat steady states. Presently there are only limited results in the literature about such solutions, cf. [35], and they are of interest as models of disk galaxies, cf. [18].

accepted.question_text: Can one establish a mathematical link between nonlinear dynamical stability and the static or stationary solutions obtained by the iterative fixed-point algorithm used for Vlasov-Poisson and Einstein-Vlasov steady states?

evidence.quote: In fact there are indications that this convergent set corresponds with solutions which are dynamically stable.

A further interesting aspect of this method is related to stability. Namely, as mentioned above, there are indications that solutions obtained by this algorithm are dynamically stable. This observation is particularly exciting in view of the open problem of non-linear stability for the spherically symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system. Hence, if a link between non-linear stability and the static solutions obtained by this algorithm can be established it would certainly be of great interest.

accepted.question_text: Can regular stationary Einstein-Vlasov solutions with ergoregions be constructed beyond the known highly rotating step-function ansatz family, in particular with total angular momentum |J| below the squared mass M² or using non-step-function ansatzes for particle energy and axial angular momentum? Here an ergoregion is the region where the stationary time-translation Killing field ∂t becomes spacelike, equivalently in the metric parametrization e^(2ν) − ρ²B²ω²e^(−2ν) < 0.

evidence.quote: The definition of an ergoregion is that the Killing field ∂t which corresponds to the time translation symmetry becomes spacelike.
In our parametrization of the metric it follows that an ergoregion is the set for which e2ν − ρ2B2ω2e−2ν < 0.
The solutions admitting ergoregions that we obtain are all highly relativistic and highly rotating, each satisfying the inequality |J | > M2.
Perhaps a different numerical scheme will be more successful in finding solutions with ergoregions and with |J | < M2.
It would be interesting to look for ergoregions in families of solutions obtained from other (non-step function) ansatzes.

accepted.question_text: For sequences of regular stationary rotating toroidal Einstein-Vlasov solutions obtained by decreasing the particle cutoff energy E₀ and tuning the angular-momentum parameter L₀, can such a sequence approach an extremal Kerr black hole with compactness Γ tending to 1, or is there instead a strict upper bound Γ<1 or an unavoidable approach to a thin-ring limit? Determine whether higher numerical resolution, a different numerical algorithm, or an analytic obstruction settles the possibility of a quasistationary transition to black holes.

evidence.quote: A central open problem is whether or not a quasistationary transition to an extremal black hole is possible.
The parameter E0 has a natural interpretation as the cutoff energy for the particles, and its presence is important for obtaining solutions with compact support [36].
Note however that the parameter L0 represents a lower bound, resulting in a solution with net angular momentum.
With more computational effort and resolution can one continue this bisection search and reach all the way to a black hole solution? It is not clear that the answer to this question is affirmative.

Hence, from this discussion an essential question arises: is a transition of stationary solutions to black hole solutions possible? Although such a transition has been established in the case of dust there is no a priori requirement that a quasistationary transition to black hole solutions must occur for solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system.

Perhaps there is a maximum value of the compactness parameter Γ which is strictly below one as in the spherically symmetric case. Perhaps solutions necessarily approach the thin ring limit when E0 is successively decreased independently of the value of L0.

accepted.question_text: Do the high-angular-momentum rotating toroidal Einstein-Vlasov solution sequences have a genuine thin-ring limiting solution whose matter distribution behaves like a Dirac-type ring, and can that limit be used analytically, as thin shells are used in spherical symmetry, to prove existence or compactness bounds for axially symmetric solutions?

evidence.quote: The thin-ring limit discussed in the section above has interesting properties of its own. As shown in [3] the limiting members of solution sequences approaching this limit appear to display a local conical geometry around the matter, reminiscent of cosmic strings.
Due to the near Dirac nature of the spatial matter distribution in this limit, proving existence of such solutions may be analytically tractable.
Perhaps a similar study is possible in the axially symmetric case by utilizing the Dirac nature of the thin ring solutions.

accepted.question_text: Can stationary three-dimensional Einstein-Vlasov solutions be found whose spatial density resembles realistic disk galaxies, meaning solutions with a density core as close to planar and as extremely flattened as observed disk galaxies, despite current constructed oblate spheroidal and rotating solutions not satisfactorily resembling such galaxies?

evidence.quote: Given the prevalence of disk galaxies in the observable universe, it is reasonable to ask whether such a morphology is represented in the space of stationary solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system.

There exist models of disk galaxies which are confined to the plane, cf. e.g. [40, 18], but it would be desirable to obtain three-dimensional solutions which are disk-like in the sense that the core of the density is as close to planar as possible.

In conclusion, our solutions do not satisfyingly resemble the extremely flattened galaxies which are observed in nature. We find it to be a central open problem to answer the question whether or not it is possible to obtain solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system which resemble realistic disk galaxies.

accepted.question_text: If disk-like Einstein-Vlasov configurations are surrounded by dark-matter-halo-like matter distributions, does this improve convergence of the numerical algorithm and support the existence of realistic flattened disk-galaxy morphologies in the Einstein-Vlasov system?

evidence.quote: A different aspect is that it is often claimed that halos of dark matter may be crucial to the pronounced flattened shape of disk galaxies.

It is a question of great importance to investigate if such halos surrounding disk-like solutions do improve the convergence of the numerical algorithm. If this turns out to be the case, it would give significant support to the established claim that disk galaxies are embedded in dark matter halos. To our knowledge this has not been investigated for the Einstein-Vlasov system and we find it to be an essential open problem.

accepted.question_text: Which choices and combinations of ansatz functions Φ(E,L_z), where E is particle energy and L_z is axial angular momentum, produce convergent stationary Einstein-Vlasov solutions with spindle-like, toroidal, or composite morphologies, and do the resulting spatial densities resemble observed composite astrophysical objects such as prolate spindle-like galaxies, active-galactic-nucleus tori, disk galaxies with central bulges, dark-matter halos, or ring galaxies?

evidence.quote: In order to construct stationary solutions it is useful to make an ansatz for the density function f on phase space, namely we assume that f depends only on the particle energy E and angular momentum Lz about the axis f(x, p) = KΦ(E, Lz).

In view of the observational evidence of these types of objects we find that a more careful study of spindle solutions and toroidal solutions is motivated, where the features of the numerical solutions should be compared with the features of the observed objects.

In 2017 galaxy surveys revealed that prolate spindle-like galaxies are much more common than previously thought [47]. In 2019 it was announced that the VLA telescope had directly imaged a toroidal structure within an active galactic nucleus [23].

It turns out to be sensitive to combine ansatz functions. Our numerical algorithm does not converge for an arbitrary non-trivial linear combination of ansatz functions even if they individually give rise to solutions.
An open issue is to understand which combinations of ansatz functions give rise to composite solutions and to find out if these solutions resemble the morphology of composite objects found in nature.
Examples of composite astrophysical objects are numerous, and include disk galaxies with a central bulge, galaxies with dark matter halos, as well as ring galaxies.

accepted.question_text: Do compactly supported stationary axially symmetric solutions of the massless Einstein-Vlasov system exist, with the density function vanishing outside a compact set so that the interior massless Vlasov solution could be glued to a vacuum exterior, and what would such solutions imply for Wheeler-type geons modeled by photon-gas matter?
accepted.context_brief: Massless axially symmetric solutions and geons

evidence.quote: A question related to the opening of this review and to the existence of compact solutions is whether or not massless axially symmetric solutions exist.

Hence, the crucial question is whether or not massless axially symmetric solutions can be constructed such that the density function vanishes outside a compact set. If so, it would be possible to glue the solution to a vacuum solution –although no explicit vacuum solution exists as in the spherically symmetric case.
Hence, the question whether or not axially symmetric solutions of the massless Einstein-Vlasov system exist is closely related to the existence of Wheeler’s original conception of geons.

accepted.question_text: Can one find general axially symmetric self-gravitating stationary Einstein-Vlasov solutions with a central black hole, beyond perturbative constructions near Kerr in which the Vlasov matter is small or close to vacuum, for example by adapting the existing numerical code to impose inner boundary conditions at the black-hole horizon?
accepted.context_brief: Self-gravitating Vlasov matter around central black holes

evidence.quote: An interesting direction in which to extend the study of regular axisymmetric stationary solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system, is to consider solutions with a central black hole. This imposes inner boundary conditions at the black hole horizon.

By the nature of the proof however, the matter must be small (close to vacuum), and it remains an open problem to find general axially symmetric self-gravitating solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov system with a central black hole.
A sensible starting place is to probe this problem numerically. One approach would be to modify the code used in [2, 3] and documented in [6].

accepted.question_text: Can numerical and analytic methods be extended to obtain general stationary axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov-Maxwell solutions with charged massive Vlasov particles interacting through the electromagnetic field, beyond perturbative regimes where total angular momentum and gravitational-field strength remain restricted?

evidence.quote: Another interesting direction of research, and possible extension of the code [6], is the addition of charge.
Allowing the particles to be charged (in addition to having mass) and interact additionally through the electromagnetic field leads to the Einstein-Vlasov-Maxwell system.

The total angular momentum and the strength of the gravitational field are still restricted, and an understanding of general solutions to the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov-Maxwell system is lacking.

accepted.question_text: Are the highly compact stationary axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov solutions stable under time evolution, and how can the very high spatial resolution needed to construct those stationary solutions be transferred to an evolution code so that simulations of their stability or collapse are practically feasible?
accepted.context_brief: Evolution and stability of highly compact solutions

evidence.quote: The question of their stability, and more generally, the fate of any axially symmetric initial data requires an evolution code.
The highly compact solutions that were constructed in [3] require very high resolution. It is an outstanding problem to determine whether or not these solutions are stable.
How can the high resolution needed for the stationary solution be carried over to the evolution problem to make a simulation practically feasible?
